content: In humans, the thigh is the anatomical region located between the pelvis and buttocks proximally, and the knee distally. It is considered a part of the lower limb. The femur, the single bone within the thigh, is exceptionally thick and robust due to its high proportion of cortical bone. This bone articulates proximally with the pelvis at the hip joint, forming a ball-and-socket joint, and distally with the tibia at the knee joint, forming a condylar joint. When viewed in cross-section, the thigh is divided into three distinct fascial compartments. These compartments are organized around the femur, which serves as the central axis, and are separated by strong connective tissue membranes known as septa. Each compartment has its own dedicated blood supply, nerve supply, and a specific group of muscles. The three compartments are as follows: The medial fascial compartment of the thigh The posterior fascial compartment of the thigh The anterior fascial compartment of the thigh The arterial blood supply to the thigh is primarily provided by the femoral artery and the obturator arterial system. Lymphatic drainage closely parallels the arterial pathways. The deep venous system of the thigh includes the femoral vein, the proximal portion of the popliteal vein, and several smaller veins. This system is a common site for proximal deep venous thrombosis. Additionally, the perforating veins (venae perforantes) connect the deep venous system to the superficial venous system, which includes the saphenous veins. The superficial venous system is often implicated in the development of varicose veins. Weakness in the thigh muscles can manifest clinically as a positive Gower's sign during physical examination.
